description: We are a team passionate about space, technology and problem solving. We bring together skills in  design, data analysis and teamwork, to create a smart map to help the first astronauts navigate and walk safely on Mars!
summary: A.R.G.O.S. is an interactive map for planning science focused exploration on Mars. Demonstrated through a Jezero crater case study, it combines terrain and mineral visualizations with route planning, spoken navigation, and simulated astronaut or rover movement. Users can inspect an area of scientific interest, mark a destination, identify mapped terrain hazards, and explore an alternative route. A selectable 72-hour environmental scenario illustrates how temperature, wind, dust, and ionized radiation conditions could affect an extravehicular activity. Drawing on NASA mission resources, A.R.G.O.S. connects scientific target selection with the safe navigation and practical decisions of a Marswalk. The prototype demonstrates an integrated planning workflow while clearly distinguishing mapped information, derived estimates, and illustrative simulations.
details:
Introduction

Future crewed missions to Mars will require astronauts to explore unfamiliar environments, identify scientifically valuable locations, and navigate challenging terrain while considering environmental conditions, astronaut safety, and mission limitations.
A.R.G.O.S. (Advanced Route Guidance & Observation System) is an interactive Martian mapping and navigation platform designed to support the planning and simulation of these exploration activities. By combining geographical, geological, and environmental information, A.R.G.O.S. allows users to investigate areas of scientific interest, evaluate potential terrain hazards, and plan routes toward selected destinations.
The current prototype focuses on Jezero Crater, an important location for investigating Mars geological history and potential past habitability. 

Exploration & Navigation Capabilities

A.R.G.O.S. brings several complementary capabilities together within a single interactive map.
The platform provides a satellite-based map of the Martian surface with multiple geographical and geological information layers. Users can examine terrain elevation and slope variations to identify potentially challenging areas, while mineral distribution layers visualize mapped spectral signatures associated with olivines, smectites, carbonates, and sulfates. These minerals are scientifically interesting because their presence and distribution can provide information about the planet's geological evolution and its past environmental conditions.
The Area Scan functionality allows users to select a specific region and analyze its characteristics. It estimates the selected surface area, identifies portions of the mapped terrain classified as potentially hazardous, and calculates the percentage of the selected map area covered by the displayed mineral spectral-signature layers. Users can also mark points of interest to identify locations that may be valuable for future scientific investigations.
For route planning, A.R.G.O.S. enables users to define a path toward a selected destination while considering mapped terrain hazards. When a route crosses an area classified as potentially dangerous, for example due to steep slopes, the system highlights the hazard and allows users to auto adjust the route to avoid it. The prototype uses a 15° slope threshold as an illustrative hazard classification, rather than an established operational safety limit for astronauts.
The platform also includes a navigation simulation for both astronauts traveling on foot and rovers. It provides estimated travel distances and durations, directional headings, and spoken navigation instructions to demonstrate how future exploration activities could be guided across the Martian surface.

Environmental Conditions & Mission Planning

In addition to geographical and geological information, A.R.G.O.S. integrates an environmental information panel displaying atmospheric temperature, wind speed, direction and gusts, atmospheric dust, and ionized radiation indicators.Users can explore a simulated environmental scenario extending up to 72 Martian hours ahead, observing how changing conditions could affect the suitability of a planned extravehicular activity. The platform also displays Martian time information and an illustrative communication-delay indicator between Mars and Earth.
The environmental scenarios are informed by historical Mars mission observations and scientific references. 

Scientific Data & Resources

The development of A.R.G.O.S. was supported by scientific information and publicly available resources from NASA missions and the United States Geological Survey (USGS). For the geographical and geological representation of Jezero Crater, NASA Mars Trek and information from the Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars (CRISM) aboard NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO-(HiRISE)) and Mars Global Surveyor (MGS-(MOLA)) were used as references for the visualization of Martian surface mineralogy. The USGS Astrogeology Science Center was also used as a reference for Martian terrain and elevation information, supporting the representation and interpretation of topographical features and potential terrain hazards. To prepare the map layers used in the application, QGIS, an open-source geographic information system, was used to work with the geographical and geological information and create the corresponding image layers. These prepared images were subsequently incorporated into A.R.G.O.S. to allow users to switch between different visualizations of the Martian surface and examine the information together. For environmental conditions, historical observations from the Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer (MEDA) instrument aboard NASA's Perseverance rover provided reference values for atmospheric temperature and wind. In particular, observations from Martian sols 65 and 66, available through NASA's Planetary Data System (PDS), were used to inform the temperature patterns and wind reference conditions represented in the simulation. The atmospheric dust scenario was informed by published observations of Martian dust storms, including findings from the 2018 global dust storm observed by NASA's Curiosity rover, together with general environmental information from NASA's Mars reference resources. These scientific references helped establish plausible environmental variations for the demonstration, rather than providing an actual prediction of future weather conditions. For the radiation indicator, published measurements from the Radiation Assessment Detector (RAD) aboard NASA's Curiosity rover were used as a historical reference. Since these observations originate from Gale Crater rather than Jezero Crater, the radiation values displayed in A.R.G.O.S. are illustrative and should not be interpreted as actual local radiation measurements at the demonstration site. Finally, NASA's Mars24 Sunclock documentation provided the scientific basis for Martian time calculations and the representation of local solar time. The communication-delay indicator is also illustrative and does not represent a live measurement of the current Earth–Mars signal travel time.

Development Tools & Super Intelligence

A.R.G.O.S. was developed as an interactive, browser-based application using Visual Studio Code as the main development environment. The development process involved extensive assistance from OpenAI ChatGPT and Google Gemini, which were used to generate and improve the application's code. The development was guided through iterative instructions and feedback, focusing on defining the desired functionalities, identifying problems, and refining the results. The project also involved selecting and examining scientific information, preparing the geographical and geological visualization layers using QGIS, and testing the application's functionality.

Future development

Potential enhancements include estimating astronaut oxygen consumption, rover energy requirements, available exploration time, and communication limitations between astronauts, rovers, and mission control. Further validation of terrain analysis and route-planning capabilities could also improve the platform's ability to support realistic exploration scenarios.

Conclusions

With continued scientific validation and technological development, A.R.G.O.S. could be an advanced decision-support platform for future human missions to Mars.
Our long-term vision is to develop A.R.G.O.S. into a platform that helps future astronauts explore Mars more safely, efficiently, and scientifically.
